# RFC-0002: The operator contract

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @wael
> **Tags:** `architecture`, `out-of-core`, `performance`

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0002:C-OVERVIEW] Overview and scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0002c-overview"></a>

An operator expressed only as an opaque stream transform cannot be scheduled out of core: it has no way to
tell the scheduler it needs points it was not handed, so it either produces silently wrong answers at every
partition boundary or forces the whole dataset into memory. Every obligation here follows from resolving
that, and from deciding who may write an operator once the contract exists.

**Scope** — what an operator declares and what the planner owes it in return; the memory ceiling it respects;
attribute projection; result honesty; who may implement one; what user-supplied logic may express; and how an
operator's origin bears on the output it produces.

**Out of scope** — preview and committed-run semantics ([RFC-0003](../rfc/RFC-0003.md)); how the environment supplies storage,
retrieval and parallelism ([RFC-0004](../rfc/RFC-0004.md)); coordinate interpretation and point references ([RFC-0005](../rfc/RFC-0005.md));
component boundaries and the rendering path ([RFC-0006](../rfc/RFC-0006.md)); editing ([RFC-0007](../rfc/RFC-0007.md)). Which operators exist,
and expression syntax.

Extension sits here rather than apart because it is the same subject viewed from outside: C-EXTENSION says
who may satisfy the contract, C-EXPRESSION says what a user may supply within it, and C-ORIGIN says what
follows when nobody has checked the contract was met. Separating them would put the contract in one document
and the constraints on meeting it in another.

The design is patterned on a physical query planner — operators declare requirements, the planner inserts
operations that satisfy them — because that is the shape that makes out-of-core scheduling tractable. It is
deliberately **not** patterned on a query *engine*: the two capabilities point clouds need and tabular
engines lack are overlapping partitions and level of detail.

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0002:C-EXEC] Operator model and requirement satisfaction (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-exec"></a>

An operator expressed only as an opaque stream transform cannot be scheduled out of core: it has no way
to tell the scheduler it needs points it was not handed, so it either produces silently wrong answers at
every partition boundary or forces the whole dataset into memory. Requirements are therefore
**declared**, and satisfying them is the planner's obligation rather than the operator's.

1. Every operator MUST declare, without being executed, the requirements it places on its input. The
   declaration MUST include:
   - the **spatial partitioning** it requires;
   - the **minimum halo width** it requires (C-HALO);
   - the **attributes** it reads (C-PROJECTION);
   - the **number of passes** it makes over its input.
2. The planner MUST insert operations that satisfy each declared requirement before the operator
   executes.
   - It MUST reject a pipeline whose declared requirements cannot be satisfied, and the rejection MUST
     name the operator and the specific unmet requirement.
   - It MUST NOT execute an operator whose requirements are unsatisfied.
3. The representation at every operator boundary MUST be an Apache Arrow record batch with no
   Strider-specific envelope, header, or sidecar.
   - An operator MUST NOT require its input to be re-encoded from a plain Arrow batch before use.
   - An operator MUST NOT emit output that requires Strider-specific decoding before an unrelated Arrow
     consumer can read it.
4. A stream's spatial properties — **partition bounds**, **level of detail**, **source partition
   identity**, and **halo width** — MUST be properties of the *stage* that produces the stream, and MUST
   NOT be fields attached to individual records or batches.
   - **Partition bounds** are the volume the stage's partition is responsible for. They are NOT the extent
     of the points the stage carries: halo points lie outside the bounds by construction, so a stage's
     bounds MUST NOT be computed from the positions it holds.
   - Bounds MUST state, for each face, whether that face is **closed** or **open**, so that membership
     (C-HALO 1) is decidable from the bounds alone. A partitioning MUST assign closedness so that every
     position within its extent lies within the bounds of exactly one of its partitions.
   - A planner MUST be able to determine every such property without reading point data.
   - **Halo membership** is not an exception, though it is carried per point. It is *derived* from those
     bounds together with the point's own position, and the column C-HALO 1 requires caches that derivation
     rather than introducing a property of the record.
5. The planner MUST NOT execute an operator whose requirements, satisfied under (2), have been altered
   since they were satisfied.
   - A partitioning satisfying a declared spatial partitioning MUST NOT be reorganised between satisfaction
     and execution. Establishing a partitioning *afresh* is not such a reorganisation: a halo exchange
     (C-COMPOSITION 2), an adaptive repartitioning ([RFC-0003:C-PARTITIONING](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-partitioning) 2), and the
     re-establishment a coordinate
     transformation requires ([RFC-0005:C-TRANSFORM](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-transform) 3) each satisfy the requirement again rather than
     invalidating it.
   - Where the planner delegates part of an evaluation to an evaluator outside its control, it MUST establish
     from that evaluator's **interface** that a partitioning handed to it cannot be reorganised — that the
     interface can express the requirement and undertake to preserve it — and MUST reject the pipeline where
     the interface cannot settle the question. Neither the evaluator's configuration nor its observed
     behaviour on any particular input MUST be treated as establishing it.
   - Where such a delegation occurs, conformance MUST be verified with that evaluator present, by the
     comparison against a single-partition reference C-HALO 4 requires. The verification is owed by whatever
     integrates the evaluator, and this item imposes none on a pipeline that delegates nothing.

#### Rationale

Declaring **pass count** matters as much as declaring halo width, and is the item most easily omitted. An
operator that summarises its input and then revisits it — the shape of morphological ground filters and of
height above ground — needs the planner to arrange two traversals *and* needs the source to be
replayable. A single stream transform expresses one pass, so nothing in its signature communicates the
second.

Requiring the planner to *name* the unmet requirement (2), rather than fail generically, is what makes an
unsatisfiable pipeline diagnosable by whoever assembled it rather than by whoever wrote the planner.

The prohibition in (3) is on the *envelope*, not on richness: a batch may carry any columns, including
ones Strider defines. What it may not do is require Strider code to be readable at all.

(4) is what lets the planner reason before reading — proving a requirement already satisfied, or
rejecting a pipeline, without touching point data. The accepted cost is that a stream is not
self-describing in isolation: a batch handed to an external consumer carries no spatial context.

(5) is the obligation (2) leaves out. (2) requires a requirement to be *satisfied*; nothing required
satisfaction to still hold when the operator ran. Measured: an analytical engine redistributed an
already-partitioned input beneath a node of its own plan, and 74 of 110 neighbour counts were wrong against a
whole-dataset reference. No stage failed, no declaration was violated, and every requirement had been
satisfied at the moment it was checked. What the measurement does *not* show is that the redistribution was
undetectable — the same evidence records that a rule placed after distribution enforcement can see such a
node. What was absent was any signal: no error, no warning, no annotation on the plan. The obligation is
therefore about who must look, not about what can be seen.

(5)'s first bullet distinguishes reorganising from re-establishing, which is the difference between a defect
and a design. Three arrangements the corpus requires or permits reorganise a partitioning on purpose, and
each re-satisfies the declaration afterwards. A rule forbidding reorganisation outright would forbid them.

(5)'s second bullet is the part that costs something, and it names *where* the property must be established
because otherwise the obligation has no observable. The test is the evaluator's interface: can a caller state
the requirement in terms the evaluator accepts, and does the evaluator undertake to keep it? For the evaluator
measured, the answer is no — its vocabulary for describing an input distribution has three forms, none of
which can say "the partitioning my source produced, intact" — so the question is settled negatively before any
run. The cheaper rule would have accepted a configuration switch instead. That relocates a correctness
property into ambient configuration, where it can be changed by someone who does not know what depends on it
and where nothing in the pipeline records the dependency. Behaviour is excluded for the same reason from the
other side: an evaluator that happens not to reorganise one input has established nothing about the next. The
accepted consequence is that work carrying a spatial partitioning is not delegated to an evaluator of that
kind, which is why an operator with a halo is not delegable.

(5)'s third bullet is conditional for a reason of layering, not of leniency. The failure is invisible in
isolation — each operator tested alone satisfies everything it declares, and the defect appears only in
composition — so the verification has to include the evaluator. But the crates that must not depend on a
query engine cannot host such a test, so the obligation is placed on whatever integrates the evaluator, and
falls away entirely where nothing is delegated.

(4) says **partition bounds** and defines them, where an earlier wording said "bounding volume" and left the
choice between two volumes open. The distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic: a halo-bearing stage's
stream *contains* points outside the partition it is responsible for, so a volume computed from the points
carried would enclose the halo — and membership derived from that volume would make every point a core point,
which is the opposite of what C-HALO 1 needs. The bounds are declared by whoever assembled the partition, not
measured from its contents.

(4)'s list once carried an exception for halo membership, on the ground that it is genuinely per-point. It is
not: membership follows from the partition bounds already listed here together with the point's own position,
so the list is exhaustive after all and the column that records membership is a cache of a derivation. That
matters beyond tidiness — an exception would have been a second kind of spatial property, and every clause
reasoning over this list would have had to say whether it meant to include it.

### [RFC-0002:C-HALO] Neighbourhood halo and partition overlap (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-halo"></a>

Normal estimation, nearest-neighbour features, outlier removal and cloth-simulation ground filtering all
need points beyond the partition being processed: a point near the edge of an octree node has neighbours
in sibling nodes and in nodes at other levels of detail. Supplying those neighbours means partitions
**overlap**, which is the one place borrowing a tabular planner's assumptions produces wrong answers
rather than slow ones.

1. Halo points supplied to satisfy an operator's declared halo width (C-EXEC 1) MUST be distinguishable
   from the partition's own points by a dedicated boolean attribute in the batch.
   - What that attribute records is fixed rather than chosen. A point handed to an operator is a **core
     point** of the partition it was handed for where its position lies within that partition's **bounds**
     (C-EXEC 4), and a **halo point** otherwise. Nothing else may decide it — not an ordering among the
     partitions whose halo reaches the point, and not a choice made wherever the partition was assembled.
   - Whether a face of the bounds includes the positions lying on it is given by the bounds themselves
     (C-EXEC 4), which state each face as closed or open. A partitioning that assigns closedness as C-EXEC 4
     requires therefore makes a point lying exactly on a boundary a core point of exactly one of the
     partitions sharing it, and leaves no position within its extent belonging to none. Coordinates are
     scaled integers and boundaries fall on chosen values, so a point lying exactly on a face is ordinary
     rather than limiting.
   - The count applies within **one** partitioning. Where a source is partitioned at several levels of
     detail, each level is its own partitioning, and a point is a core point of one partition per level.
   - The attribute is therefore a **cache** of a property the batch already determines, and its value MUST
     agree with that property at every point. Where the two disagree, the attribute is wrong.
   - The attribute MUST be dedicated to this purpose. Recording halo membership by overloading an attribute
     that already carries a meaning of its own MUST NOT be treated as satisfying this.
   - An operator MAY read halo points. It MUST NOT write the attribute: membership is not the operator's
     to assign, and writing it can only put the cache at odds with the property it caches.
   - An operator that alters point positions MUST either apply the same alteration to the partition's
     bounds, or declare that the partitioning it was given does not hold of its output. Applying it
     to the volume is sufficient only where doing so preserves membership, the declared halo width and
     partition identity together; where it does not, the partitioning MUST be established afresh
     ([RFC-0005:C-TRANSFORM](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-transform) 3) before any operator declaring a nonzero halo width consumes the output.
   - An operator MAY carry halo points to its output, still marked as halo, only where that output is
     consumed by another operator of the same pipeline declaring a nonzero halo width. Otherwise its output
     MUST contain no halo points.
   - The halo attribute MUST NOT be present in a pipeline's final output.
   - Within a batch, every core point MUST precede every halo point.
2. A partitioning that carries a nonzero halo MUST NOT be treated as a disjoint partitioning.
   - Before any operation whose correctness depends on each point appearing in exactly one partition —
     partial-then-final aggregation, counting, summation, mean — the planner MUST either remove the halo
     or reject the pipeline.
3. An operator's declared halo width MUST be sufficient for its own neighbourhood definition at every
   point it emits.
   - Where the operator's neighbourhood is defined by a count of neighbours rather than a distance, the
     declared width MUST bound that neighbourhood for the densities the operator accepts, or the operator
     MUST declare its output approximate under C-APPROX 1.
   - Where the operator's neighbourhood is **mediated by a summary** — a later pass reads a gridded summary an
     earlier pass built, rather than reading points directly — the operator MUST declare the summary's
     resolution and the **reach** of that later pass, as a count of summary cells. The planner MUST then supply
     a halo width of at least *(reach + 1)* multiplied by the resolution.
   - The planner MAY reduce that to *reach* multiplied by the resolution only where it has established that
     every partition boundary coincides with a summary cell boundary. Divisibility of the partition extent by
     the resolution MUST NOT be treated as establishing it: a grid may divide the extent exactly and still
     straddle every boundary if its origin is offset.
4. Conformance to (3) MUST be verified, for each operator declaring a nonzero halo width, by comparing
   output computed over multiple partitions against output computed with the input in a single partition.
   - Where the operator does not declare its output approximate, the two MUST agree under whichever regime its
     reductions use: bit-identically where they accumulate associatively ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 5); within the
     declared accumulation quantum where one is declared ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 7); and, where the operator
     has declared that its values admit no associative form ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 5), within a tolerance the
     operator declares as a function of the number of values combined per emitted point. A difference beyond
     the applicable figure is evidence the declared width is too small.
   - That third tolerance MUST NOT be declared where an associative form is available, and MUST NOT be
     widened to absorb a difference an insufficient halo caused. It exists only because combining one
     neighbourhood in two different orders can differ in the last place, which is a property of the
     arithmetic rather than of the halo.
   - Where it does declare its output approximate, the divergence MUST be bounded and that bound MUST be
     verified.
5. Removing a halo MUST reduce the batch to the contiguous range of its core points, without rewriting the
   attributes it retains (C-MATERIALISATION 2).
   - A stage that removes a halo MUST first verify that (1)'s ordering holds of the batch it was given, and
     MUST reject a batch that violates it, naming the batch.
   - It MUST NOT instead gather the core points from a mis-ordered batch. The gather is what
     C-MATERIALISATION 1 forbids, and reducing a mis-ordered batch to a range would silently emit halo
     points and drop core points.
6. Conformance to (1)'s agreement and to (5) MUST be verified by the memory-identity comparison
   C-MATERIALISATION 4 defines, together with a check that the point count after removal equals the batch's
   core point count, and a check that the halo attribute agrees with (1) at every point when evaluated
   against the partition's bounds, including the closedness those bounds state for each face.
   - The count check is not redundant: memory identity holds for a range taken at the wrong offset or
     length, so it cannot detect a range that is shared but wrong.
   - The agreement check MUST be a conformance verification and MUST NOT be imposed on every batch a stage
     removes a halo from. Evaluating (1) needs the position attributes, so requiring it at each removal
     would oblige a pipeline to carry those attributes through stages that read none of them — the waste
     C-PROJECTION exists to remove. The stage that assembles a partition holds the positions already.
7. A stage that carries halo points to its output under (1) MUST declare that it does, as a property of the
   stage (C-EXEC 4).
   - A planner MUST reject a pipeline in which a stage declaring carry-forward has a consumer that declares a
     zero halo width, and MUST reject one in which the last stage declaring carry-forward is not followed by a
     removal under (5). Each rejection MUST name the stage.
   - Conformance MUST be verified by presenting a pipeline of each rejected shape and confirming the
     rejection, not only by presenting conformant pipelines and observing that they run.

#### Rationale

Halo membership is per-point but not primitive: it follows from the point's own position together with the
partition bounds C-EXEC 4 already makes a property of the producing stage. That is why (1) fixes the geometry
first and the column second. An earlier form of this clause named only the column, which left *what makes a
point core* to whoever assembled the partition — and with scaled-integer coordinates and boundaries on chosen
values, a point lying exactly on a shared boundary is common rather than exotic. Two assemblers could decide
it oppositely, both conform, and between them duplicate or lose it: the silent class (2) exists to prevent.
The half-open convention costs nothing and closes it. Which limit is the closed one is arbitrary; that it is
stated is not.

The exception for the partitioning's own outer limit is not a nicety. A half-open rule applied to *every*
limit gives a point on the outermost upper boundary no owning partition at all, and (5)'s range reduction then
discards it from every one — so the count guarantee below would be false for exactly those points. They are
not hypothetical: a LAS header records the maximum coordinate on each axis, so a point attaining it exists by
construction in most files. Closing the outer limit costs one comparison and is the difference between a rule
that partitions the input and one that quietly loses a face of it.

Fixing the geometry as the definition is also what makes the column **falsifiable**. A stored label with no
stated meaning cannot be wrong, so an obligation about it cannot be checked; a cache of a defined property
can be wrong, and (6) checks it.

The column is nonetheless kept rather than derived at each use, for a reason that has nothing to do with the
label. What cannot be recovered from partition bounds is (1)'s **ordering** — which rows form the leading
contiguous run is not a geometric fact — and the core count that makes removal a range (5) is unfalsifiable
without something independent to check it against. The column is that something, at one bit per point.
Deriving membership instead would cost the position attributes in every projection reaching a halo-bearing
stage, including for operators that read none of them. Carrying it as an ordinary boolean column also keeps
C-EXEC 3 intact — an external Arrow consumer sees a normal column, not an envelope.

The requirement that the attribute be *dedicated* is there because the cheap alternative has been tried at
scale. LAStools' `lastile` records buffer membership by setting each buffer point's **withheld** flag — an
attribute whose defined meaning in the LAS specification is that a return is unreliable — and the United
States Geological Survey has since published guidance restricting what that flag may be taken to mean. An
overloaded attribute makes halo membership
indistinguishable from whatever else the attribute records, and exports the ambiguity to every consumer of
the file.

**Never relabel** is what prevents duplication, and it is a narrower rule than never-emit. A point near a
boundary is supplied to every partition whose halo reaches it; if each turned it into a core point, it would
appear several times in the output. Carrying it forward *still marked as halo* duplicates nothing, because it
is removed before any operation depending on disjointness (2) and before the pipeline's output. What the rule
guarantees is that a partitioned neighbourhood computation produces the same core point count as its
whole-dataset equivalent.

The position bullet exists because (1) defines membership geometrically, which makes displacement a way of
changing membership without touching any label — a path a clause naming only the label could not describe.
But it is stated as a duty to keep the volume and the positions *together*, not as a prohibition on moving
points, because the prohibition would have been wrong twice over: it would have forbidden the partition-wise
reformulations C-MEMORY 2 expressly admits, and it would have treated a whole class of safe operators as
unsafe.

The safe class is the one where the alteration is an **isometry**, and three quantities have to survive for a
partitioning to still hold of the output. An isometry preserves all three at once. Distances, so a declared
halo width is still a width. Containment, so no point changes which side of a boundary it lies on. And
partition identity, which comes from spatial index node keys rather than from coordinates, so the fixed
reduction order [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 3 derives from those keys is untouched. Moving the bounds by
the same isometry therefore costs nothing and needs no re-establishment. A translation is the extreme case:
coordinates are stored as scaled integers about an offset, so translating is a change of offset with no
per-point arithmetic at all and — unlike a reprojection — no requantisation, so the accumulation quantum
survives too.

The bullet requires those three properties rather than naming the permitted transformations, because one
question is deliberately left open. A general rotation maps an axis-aligned volume to an oriented one, so
carrying it exactly preserves all three but obliges the partitioning to admit oriented volumes, while
replacing it with its axis-aligned bound reintroduces overlap between neighbours and with it the very
duplication this rule prevents. Translations and quarter turns are exact under either treatment. Stating the
properties lets an implementation carry the volume wherever it genuinely can, and fall back to
re-establishment where it cannot, without this clause having to settle the shape of a bounding volume.

The non-disjointness rule (2) exists because the failure is silent. An aggregation over a halo
partitioning does not fail, log, or crash — it returns a plausible number, too large in proportion to the
ratio of boundary points to interior points, which is exactly the ratio that grows as partitions get
smaller. Making it a *planner* obligation rather than an operator-author convention is deliberate: it
cannot be left to whoever writes the next aggregate to remember.

(3) is the obligation C-EXEC 1 does not cover. C-EXEC 1 requires a width to be *declared*; this requires
it to be *right*, which is a different claim and the one that can be wrong while everything appears to
work. A k-nearest-neighbour radius depends on local density, so an operator cannot always bound it in
advance — hence the escape to approximation rather than a prohibition.

(3)'s summary bullets exist because a two-pass operator's reach is not visible in the neighbourhood its second
pass appears to use. Reading a gridded summary looks like reading one cell, and needs points from beyond the
partition for two separate reasons: a cell overlapping the partition boundary is incomplete without the
neighbouring partition's points, and any cell the pass reads beyond its own must exist at all. Both are
satisfied by a *point* halo, which is why this needs no second kind of halo and no second unit — the reach
converts to a distance through the resolution and stays commensurable with every other declared width,
including the sum C-COMPOSITION 3 takes.

The split of responsibility is deliberate and is what the two bullets encode. *Reach* and *resolution* are the
operator's: they describe what its own second pass does. The extra cell is the *partitioning's*, because
whether a cell straddles a boundary is a fact about where boundaries fall — which an operator has no business
knowing. So the operator declares two numbers and the planner computes the width.

The extra cell is a MUST and its removal a MAY because of what was measured. The straddle term is a matter of
alignment, and it is *not* divisibility: a grid whose resolution divided the partition extent exactly still
needed half a cell of halo when its origin was offset by half a cell, and six tenths when offset by four
tenths. A rule keyed on divisibility would therefore supply too little, silently, in a configuration that
looks aligned. The safe bound is the full cell — an overhang is strictly less than one cell wherever
boundaries do not coincide — and the reduction is available only against the predicate that actually holds.

(7) closes what (1)'s third bullet opened, and it has to be a *declaration* to be closable at all. A flat
prohibition on emitting halo points was checkable by looking at outputs. Permitting a carry-forward moved the
condition onto the relationship between stages — and whether a stage carries a halo forward is a fact about
its output data, while whether its consumer wants one is a fact about a declaration. Checking a conjunction of
the two would mean inspecting data to validate a plan. Requiring the carrying stage to *declare* it puts both
halves in the same register, so a planner can decide the question on the pipeline graph before anything runs,
which is where C-EXEC 2 already decides everything else of this kind.

(7)'s last bullet is there because this obligation is a rejection, and a rejection is the one kind of
requirement that a passing test suite can silently fail to exercise. Conformant pipelines running proves
nothing about a planner that never rejects anything.

(4) is the verification that cannot be faked, and its three regimes exist because an earlier form required
the two runs to agree *exactly* and the evidence does not support that. What a sufficient halo makes lossless
is the **neighbourhood set**: every emitted point sees the neighbours a whole-dataset run would have given it.
It does not make the arithmetic identical. Measured, a mean over a neighbourhood agreed to within one part in
ten thousand of a millionth of a millionth — about one unit in the last place — at a sufficient width *and* at
a composed-sufficient width, because the same values were summed in a different order. An exact-agreement rule
would therefore have failed a conformant operator.

The regimes are ordered so that the loosest is hardest to reach. Where values admit an associative form
[RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 5 already requires one, and then agreement is bit-identical with nothing to tolerate.
The declared tolerance is available only to an operator that has declared, under the same item, that its
values admit no associative form — which is a real class: an eigen-decomposition over a covariance matrix has
no useful associative accumulator. Without the third regime that class had no reachable criterion at all,
since such an operator has no accumulation quantum either. What the tolerance must not become is a place to
hide an insufficient halo, which is why it is a stated function of the neighbourhood size rather than a
constant: an inadequate width produces a difference that does not scale that way.

(1)'s ordering bullet exists to make (5) achievable, and the obligation is on the batch *handed to an
operator* rather than on every batch in existence, because the stage that assembles a partition is the one
that can satisfy it without paying for it. Why an in-batch ordering contract is preferable to the
alternatives is argued in the accompanying architecture decision.

(5)'s two bullets are the refusal half. Reducing a batch to a range is correct only if the range is the core
points, and a plain Arrow batch cannot express its own row order in its schema (C-EXEC 3), so nothing but
(5)'s check stands between a mis-ordered batch and a plausible wrong answer. The prohibition on gathering
instead is what stops an implementation recovering from a violation by paying the cost (5) was written to
remove, and thereby concealing a defect in whatever produced the batch.

(1)'s third bullet is what makes a chain of neighbourhood operators possible at all: the halo has to survive
between them, and C-COMPOSITION governs how wide it must be. The condition on it, and the declaration (7)
requires of a stage that uses it, are what keep the narrower rule from being a weaker one.

### [RFC-0002:C-COMPOSITION] Composed halo width across a chain of operators (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-composition"></a>

C-HALO 3 makes each operator answer for its own halo width. A planner that satisfies every declaration
individually has therefore satisfied every operator — and can still have supplied too little, because halo
widths compose along a chain while no single declaration accounts for the chain. The result is wrong at every
partition boundary with no operator in breach of anything. Why that happens, and what avoiding it costs, is
argued in the accompanying architecture decision; the obligation is here, and it is the planner's.

1. Operators form a **dependent chain** where each after the first reads an attribute the previous one
   derives ([RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 1). Reading only attributes the previous operator passed through
   does not make a chain.
2. A planner MUST evaluate a dependent chain by exactly one of the following, and MUST NOT evaluate it by
   any other arrangement:
   - **composed halo** — supply one halo whose width is at least the sum of the chain's declared widths, and
     remove it once, after the last operator;
   - **halo exchange** — supply each operator its own declared width and re-supply the halo between
     operators, from partition outputs that are all complete.
   - Supplying each operator its own declared width *without* re-supplying between them MUST NOT be used. It
     satisfies every operator's declaration and is the arrangement this clause exists to forbid.
3. The **composed halo width** of a dependent chain is the sum of its operators' halo widths, taking for each
   operator the width C-HALO 3 makes sufficient — which for a summary-mediated operator the planner derives
   rather than reads. A planner MUST compute it before any operator in the chain executes.
   - The partition-alignment term C-HALO 3 adds for a summary-mediated operator MUST be counted once for the
     chain, not once per operator. It is a property of where partition boundaries fall rather than of any
     operator, so counting it per operator would over-supply and could turn (4) into a spurious rejection.
   - Where a chain is split into segments, each evaluated over one supplied halo with an exchange between
     segments, the width supplied to a segment MUST be at least that segment's sum.
   - Where an operator's neighbourhood is defined by a count of neighbours rather than a distance, its
     contribution is the width it declares under C-HALO 3. An operator that cannot bound its neighbourhood,
     and so declares its output approximate, MUST NOT be admitted to a dependent chain evaluated by
     composed halo, because its reach is unbounded and no sum exists.
4. A planner MUST reject a pipeline whose composed halo width it cannot supply within the memory ceiling
   ([RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 1), naming the chain and the width required.
   - It MUST NOT satisfy a composed halo width by supplying a halo whose size is a function of the
     dataset's total point count.
   - Halo exchange MUST NOT be used to evade that ceiling either: the intermediate outputs it holds between
     operators are subject to the same bound, and MUST be spilled through the host storage interface
     ([RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 4) rather than accumulated in memory.
5. The arrangement used and the halo width supplied MUST be recorded in the evaluation configuration
   ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 4).
6. Conformance to (2) and (3) MUST be verified, for a dependent chain of at least two operators declaring
   nonzero halo widths, by comparing its partitioned output against the same chain computed with the input
   in a single partition, at two supplied widths.
   - At a width at or above the composed halo width, the two MUST agree on the terms C-HALO 4 states.
   - At a width that satisfies every operator's individual declaration but is below the composed halo width,
     the two MUST be shown to differ, and the count of differing points and the largest divergence MUST be
     reported. A width below any individual declaration MUST NOT be used for this case: it tests C-HALO 3
     rather than this clause.
   - Where the below-composed case does not differ, the verification has established nothing and MUST NOT
     be recorded as passing.

#### Rationale

(1) is what keeps the obligation from applying where it is not needed, and the distinction is one the corpus
already draws. Widths compose because each operator spends a border of validity the previous one produced —
so where the second operator reads only pass-through attributes, its input near the boundary is as good as
the source's, the largest single declaration suffices, and no divergence exists for (6) to find. Gating on a
*data dependency* rather than on execution order also closes the obvious evasion: fusing two operators, or
streaming batches from one into the next, changes the scheduling and not the arithmetic.

(2) is written as a closed set, with the third arrangement named rather than left to follow from (3), because
a prohibition a reader has to derive is one an implementation can miss. Both permitted arrangements are exact,
and which is cheaper depends on the pipeline, so the clause requires the choice to be made rather than making
it.

(3)'s first bullet is there because the quantities being summed have different owners. An operator's reach is
its own and composes along the chain; the alignment term belongs to the partitioning, and a chain crosses the
same boundaries however many operators it contains. Counting it once is what keeps the sum a statement about
reach rather than about arithmetic.

(3)'s segment bullet exists because the two arrangements in (2) are endpoints rather than alternatives: a
four-operator chain may be split into two pairs with one exchange between them, and that is often the
cheapest option. Stating the rule per segment rather than per pipeline is what admits it.

(3)'s last bullet is the case with no answer. An operator whose neighbourhood is a count rather than a
distance can be admitted alone under C-HALO 3, which lets it declare a width that bounds its neighbourhood
for the densities it accepts, or else declare its output approximate. In a dependent chain the second option
has no meaning: an unbounded reach contributes an unbounded term, so there is no width to supply and no
approximation bound to state. Excluding it is honest where quietly summing what it happens to declare would
not be.

(4) is the refusal half. A composed width grows with the chain, so it can exceed what a partition-bounded
ceiling permits, and the clause has to say what happens then rather than leaving a planner to supply what it
cannot afford. It has to say it about *both* arrangements: exchange trades the wide halo for intermediate
state held across every partition, which reaches the same ceiling from the other side.

(6)'s second bullet is the part that makes the verification able to fail. Comparing only at or above the
composed width would pass for an implementation that supplied the sum, for one that supplied a hundred times
the sum, and for one handed a dataset with no points near a boundary. Requiring the below-composed case to
differ establishes that the comparison is sensitive to the thing it claims to check — and requiring that
case to still satisfy every individual declaration is what makes it a test of this clause rather than of
C-HALO 3. The prohibition in the third bullet is there because the honest outcome of a non-differing
below-composed case is that the input was inadequate, not that the implementation conformed.

### [RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION] Single materialisation and pass-through attributes (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-materialisation"></a>

Out-of-core processing is only worth doing if it is fast, and what dominates a columnar pipeline is not
arithmetic but writing the same bytes a second time. A point is decoded into Arrow arrays once; every stage
after that either shares those bytes or pays to copy them. The copy is invisible in results — the answers
are identical, only slower — so nothing downstream ever complains, and a pipeline can lose most of its
throughput to work no test is looking for. This clause exists to make the difference checkable.

1. An operator MUST NOT rewrite an attribute it passes through, where the points it emits are a contiguous
   range of the points it was given.
   - An attribute is **derived** where the operator's output for it differs from its input for at least one
     emitted point. Every other output attribute is **passed through**.
   - Where the points an operator emits are not a contiguous range of its input, it MUST rewrite each
     passed-through attribute at most once.
2. A stage that reduces a batch to a contiguous range of its points MUST do so by adjusting which points
   the batch describes, and MUST NOT produce new memory for the attributes it retains.
3. Obligations (1) and (2) are scoped to a single process, with no spill ([RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 4) and no
   serialisation between the two states being compared.
   - Where a spill or serialisation intervenes, memory identity cannot hold and neither obligation applies.
   - A stage MUST NOT be relieved of (1) or (2) by introducing a spill or serialisation that the memory
     ceiling did not require.
4. Conformance to (1) and (2) MUST be verified by comparing, for every passed-through attribute, the
   identity of the memory backing it before and after.
   - The comparison MUST cover every buffer of the attribute's representation transitively: its value
     buffers, any validity bitmap, any child arrays, and any dictionary values. Comparing only the first
     value buffer is insufficient — an attribute of a nested or dictionary-encoded type holds none of its
     content there and would pass the check vacuously.
   - Both states MUST be live at the moment of comparison, because a freed allocation may be handed back
     at the same address.
   - The comparison MUST be of memory identity, not of attribute values. Equal values are what a copy also
     produces, so a value comparison cannot distinguish the conformant case from the one (1) forbids.

#### Rationale

**Derived is defined by values, not by declaration** (1), because the alternative does not survive contact
with an author. If an operator declared which attributes it derives, the declaration would be the escape:
an operator that rebuilds every column could call every column derived and be conformant by construction,
and no test could contradict it. Defining derived as *differing for at least one emitted point* makes the
claim falsifiable — an attribute declared derived whose values match its input everywhere is a detectable
lie — and costs no new declaration surface.

The contiguity condition in (1) is what keeps the obligation honest rather than impossible. An operator
whose surviving points are scattered — cropping to an arbitrary region, filtering on an attribute — cannot
share memory with its input at all, and demanding it would make the clause unimplementable and therefore
ignored. What such an operator can still be held to is the *at most once* bound in the second bullet: one
gather, not a gather per stage.

(3) exists because (1) and (2) would otherwise contradict [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 4, which permits spilling
to satisfy a memory ceiling. Address identity cannot survive a spill and reload, so an implementation
obeying one clause would breach the other. The second bullet is what stops the scope becoming a loophole:
spilling is permitted to bound memory, not to escape this clause.

(4) is the verification, and its first bullet is the part that is easy to get wrong in a way that reports
success. In a typical Arrow implementation the null bitmap is not among an array's data buffers, a struct
array has no data buffers at all, and a dictionary's values live in a child array — so a check that
compares one buffer per attribute passes vacuously for exactly the types where a rewrite is most likely.
The requirement to compare transitively is what makes the check mean what it says.

The obligation is written as a prohibition on rewriting rather than as a permission to share because the
wrong implementation is the obvious one. Selecting points by predicate is the natural way to express
"these points and not those", it produces exactly the right answer, and it rewrites every retained
attribute. Nothing about the output reveals it. Whether an in-batch ordering contract is preferable to the
alternatives that avoid needing one is a comparative question, argued in the accompanying architecture
decision rather than here.

### [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY] Bounded memory and admissible operators (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-memory"></a>

Bounded memory is the whole of Strider's differentiation from tools that treat a point cloud as an
in-memory object. A guarantee holding for *some* operators is not one a user can rely on when assembling
a pipeline, so the bound is a property of the operator set, enforced by excluding operators that cannot
meet it.

1. Every registered operator MUST execute within a peak memory ceiling determined only by its configured
   partition size, its declared halo width (C-EXEC 1), the declared size of any summary it builds, and the
   declared size of any index it builds over a partition.
   - That ceiling MUST NOT be a function of the dataset's total point count.
   - What makes a summary's declared size admissible, and where a summary must be built, is C-SUMMARY.
   - An index's declared size MUST be bounded by the partition size and the declared halo width. An index
     whose size is bounded only by the dataset is not admissible under this item.
2. An operator whose formulation requires simultaneous access to the entire dataset, or an unbounded
   number of passes over it, MUST NOT be registered as a built-in operator.
   - This excludes iterative pairwise registration, global surface reconstruction, and whole-cloud
     relaxation methods **in their published whole-dataset forms**.
   - A partition-wise reformulation with a declared halo is admissible under (1), and MUST then disclose
     its divergence under C-APPROX 1.
3. An operator that does not satisfy (1) MUST NOT be reachable without the caller having distinguished it
   from a bounded operator first.
   - Such an operator MUST report its own memory ceiling.
4. Spill to persistent storage is a permitted strategy for satisfying (1), and MUST be obtained through
   the host storage interface ([RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 1) rather than from the filesystem directly.
5. Conformance to (1) MUST be verified by processing inputs of at least two sizes differing by at least an
   order of magnitude, the larger exceeding available memory, and demonstrating that peak memory does not
   scale with input size.
6. Where a pipeline delegates part of its evaluation to an **external evaluator** — anything that computes
   over the pipeline's data without being one of its operators — the pipeline's peak memory MUST be bounded by
   a declared figure, and that figure MUST NOT be a function of the dataset's total point count.
   - The stage that delegates MUST supply the external evaluator a memory bound, and MUST NOT delegate to
     one that cannot be given a bound. An evaluator that *refuses* work on reaching its bound satisfies
     this; one that exceeds it silently does not.
   - An external evaluator satisfying its bound by spilling to storage it acquires for itself does not
     satisfy (4). A library crate subject to (4) MUST NOT depend on such an evaluator.
   - Where such a delegation occurs, conformance MUST be verified by (5)'s protocol applied to the pipeline
     including the delegated work, by whatever integrates the evaluator. Measuring the registered operators
     alone MUST NOT be treated as satisfying this, and this item imposes no verification on a pipeline that
     delegates nothing.

#### Rationale

Stating the ceiling as a function of declared quantities rather than a fixed byte figure keeps (1)
testable while letting an operator be configured for the machine it runs on: the test is that peak memory
stays flat as input grows, not that it stays under a particular number.

(1)'s two later bullets name what each term of the ceiling has to be bounded by, and defer the summary case to
C-SUMMARY because it needed more room than a bullet: one common summary has no admissible size at all unless
it is built per partition, which is an obligation about *where* work happens rather than about how much memory
it uses. The index term is stated here rather than deferred because it has no such subtlety — an index over a
partition is bounded by the partition.

Both are *declared* sizes rather than measured ones, which is what makes (5) a test of a claim rather than an
observation. An operator that declares nothing has not satisfied (1) by using little memory on one occasion.

(6) closes a hole that opened when part of an evaluation began to be delegated, and the hole was in the
*subject*. (1) binds every registered operator, and an evaluator performing delegated work is not an operator
of the pipeline at all — so a pipeline could conform in every item while its peak memory was set by something
no item reached. (6) identifies the evaluator by what it does rather than by what it is not, because
"registered" is a term this specification uses without defining and a negation of it would inherit that. This
clause's own opening sentence is what fails first: a guarantee holding for some of the work is not one a user
can rely on when assembling a pipeline. The same correction was needed for the same reason in the projection
obligations, where a set computed from the operators alone did not see the delegated tail either.

(6) states its own declared figure rather than reusing (1)'s ceiling, because (1)'s ceiling is not a quantity
an evaluation has. It is parameterised by an operator's *own* configured partition size, halo width, summary
size and index size, and a pipeline has no single value for any of them. What (6) borrows from (1) is the
property that matters — independence from the dataset's point count — not the arithmetic.

(6)'s first bullet admits refusal deliberately, and admits it because refusal is the only enforcement that
was actually observed. An external evaluator given a bound below what its work required *refused*; no run was
observed completing inside a bound that bit, and no peak-memory figure for such an evaluator was recorded at
all. Writing the bullet as though enforcement meant graceful containment would have claimed more than the
measurement supports — and would have made (5)'s protocol, which requires an input exceeding available
memory, mandate an outcome the only measured evaluator does not produce.

(6)'s second bullet is where delegation stops being available to the portable core. An evaluator of this kind
acquires its spill store itself: the caller may supply directories, but there is no store abstraction to
inject, so a caller-supplied store in the sense (4) requires cannot be given. Whether an evaluator's spill
counts as satisfying (4) is therefore decidable from its interface rather than from its behaviour, which is
what makes this checkable before anything runs.


### [RFC-0002:C-SUMMARY] Summary size and where a summary is built (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-summary"></a>

C-MEMORY 1 fixes an operator's ceiling partly by "the declared size of any summary it builds", which presumes
every summary has a size that can be declared. The commonest one does not. A gridded ground surface is sized
by the region it spans, and a region is a property of the dataset — so the figure an author would write down
survives until someone runs the operator over a larger survey. Two-pass operators are where bounded memory is
either real or merely stated, and this is what makes the difference checkable.

1. A summary's size is **declarable** only where it is bounded by a function of the partition size, the
   declared halo width, and the summary's own resolution — and by nothing about the data.
   - A size bounded only by the dataset's extent is not declarable. Extent is a property of the dataset, and a
     fully occupied grid grows with it.
   - A size bounded only by how many points the dataset contains is not declarable.
2. For a summary on a regular grid, the declared size MUST be the number of cells the partition and its halo
   **span** at that resolution, whether or not every cell is occupied.
   - Declaring the observed occupancy instead MUST NOT be treated as satisfying (1). Occupancy rises with
     density; the span does not.
3. An operator MUST build a summary per partition wherever a summary over the whole extent would have no
   declarable size under (1).
   - The per-partition summary MUST be built from the partition's own points together with the halo C-HALO 3
     requires for a summary-mediated neighbourhood, so that every cell the operator's later pass reads from a
     core point holds the value a whole-extent summary would have held.
4. Conformance to (1) through (3) MUST be verified by processing inputs of at least two sizes differing by at
   least an order of magnitude, as C-MEMORY 5 requires, and measuring the peak **total** summary residency
   across the run.
   - That residency MUST NOT scale with input size, and MUST remain within the size declared under (2).
   - The operator's output over multiple partitions MUST also agree with its output over a single partition,
     on the terms C-HALO 4 states.
   - Agreement alone MUST NOT be treated as satisfying this. An implementation that built the whole-extent
     summary would agree too, so residency is the only part that can fail — and it MUST be measured as a
     total, because an implementation holding one global grid can report a per-partition slice of it and show
     a flat figure.

#### Rationale

Two wrong definitions were tried before (1), and each is worth recording because each looks right.

*Bounding a summary by its resolution and the extent it covers is not a bound.* Holding resolution and density
fixed and growing a survey fourfold grows a fully occupied grid sixteenfold. A figure that scales with how
large the survey is fails C-MEMORY 1's independence from the dataset as surely as a point count does.

*Declaring the occupancy of a sparse grid is not a bound either.* A grid stored sparsely holds a cell per
occupied cell, so at a resolution finer than the point spacing its occupancy rises with density even over a
fixed partition — measured, a per-partition sparse summary grew by nearly a factor of three as the input grew
fourfold, at unchanged extent and unchanged partitioning.

(2) is what does work, and its usefulness goes beyond being true. The span is fixed by the partition, the halo
and the resolution, and a sparse grid can never exceed it — so declaring the span makes the ceiling truthful.
It also removes any need to decide which regime a resolution falls in: coarse grids saturate and fine ones do
not, but the span is the declared size in both, so no implementation has to detect the boundary and no clause
has to define it.

(3) restricts *where* a summary is computed, not what an operator may compute. Nothing here forbids a gridded
ground surface at any resolution; what is forbidden is building one over the whole extent, whose span is a
dataset property. Its bullet is why the restriction costs no accuracy — a per-partition summary built with the
halo C-HALO 3 derives holds, in every cell the later pass reads, the value the whole-extent summary would have
held, so partitioning the summary is exact rather than an approximation to disclose. Why an analytical engine's
own grouped aggregate is the wrong place to compute such a summary is a comparative question, argued in the
accompanying architecture decision.

(4) borrows C-MEMORY 5's two-size protocol rather than inventing one, and its last bullet is what makes the
check able to fail. Output agreement is what a conformant implementation and a whole-extent one have in
common, so residency is the only observable that separates them — and it has to be a total, because an
implementation holding one global grid can report a per-partition slice and show a flat figure while holding
the whole thing.

### [RFC-0002:C-PROJECTION] Attribute projection (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-projection"></a>

An operator already declares the attributes it reads (C-EXEC 1). That declaration is a projection, so a
source need never materialise more than the pipeline uses — and requiring the projection to be invisible
in the results turns it into a test of whether those declarations are honest.

1. The planner MUST compute the set of attributes a pipeline requires, and MUST supply it to the source as a
   projection.
   - The set is the union of the attributes the pipeline's operators declare (C-EXEC 1) and the attributes
     required by anything the pipeline's output is delegated to.
   - Where a delegated consumer states its own required attributes, the planner MUST use that statement rather
     than assume the whole output is required. Where it states none, the planner MUST assume all of it.
2. A source MUST accept a projection.
   - It MUST NOT materialise attributes outside the projection into the batches it emits.
3. A projection MUST NOT change results.
   - A pipeline evaluated with and without projection MUST produce identical output.

#### Rationale

No new declaration is needed for any of this: C-EXEC 1 already requires an operator to state the
attributes it reads, for scheduling reasons, so projection is available at no additional specification
cost.

The union in (1) exists because a pipeline's operators are not always the last thing to read its output. Where
the output is delegated — to an analytical engine, to an export — that consumer knows which attributes it
needs, and it is the only party that does. Computing the projection from the operators alone would then
materialise attributes nobody reads, which is the waste projection exists to remove. The measured case is a
delegated aggregate that required two attributes: unioned with the three its neighbourhood operator declared,
the source built five columns and skipped three, and the saving is at decode rather than at any later stage.

The second bullet's fallback is the conservative direction on purpose. A consumer that says nothing about its
requirements might read anything, and a projection that guessed narrow would change results — which (3)
forbids. Assuming everything is required is slower and cannot be wrong.

The achievable saving differs sharply by format, and is worth recording so it is not over-estimated. In a
columnar format, unrequested columns are never read from storage at all. In LAS and LAZ, point records are
row-oriented and a compressed chunk is a unit — the decompressor must run over the record stream to
recover any field — so the saving is in materialisation into Arrow arrays rather than in decompression or
in bytes read. Column-aware access is therefore an argument for prioritising a columnar storage path
rather than an optimisation of LAZ, which is worth knowing before effort is spent on a decoder in
expectation of columnar gains.

(3) is the part that earns its place. An operator reading an attribute it did not declare produces
different output under projection, so requiring identity makes an under-declared attribute set detectable
rather than latent — the same shape of check that [RFC-0001:C-CONFORMANCE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-conformance) applies to halo width.

### [RFC-0002:C-APPROX] Approximate results and disclosure (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-approx"></a>

Partition-wise computation with a finite halo does not reproduce the whole-dataset answer, and neither
does computation on reduced-resolution input. Both are acceptable engineering trade-offs and unacceptable
surprises. The users this serves make decisions with the output — timber volume, canopy metrics, terrain
models feeding downstream analysis.

1. An operator whose result differs from the result of its whole-dataset, full-resolution formulation MUST
   declare its output **approximate**.
   - The declaration MUST identify the **kind** of divergence, not merely its presence.
   - It MUST document the conditions under which the difference arises.
2. A pipeline containing at least one such operator MUST declare its own output approximate.
3. A user-facing surface MUST NOT present approximate output without indicating that it is approximate.
4. An **evaluation** reduced below the whole dataset at full resolution MUST declare its output approximate,
   on the same terms as (1).
   - The reductions that trigger this, and the kinds they correspond to, are
     [RFC-0003:C-RESOLUTION](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-resolution) 1 and 3.

#### Rationale

Ground classification computed per tile disagrees with a whole-cloud run along tile seams; a normal
estimated near a partition edge is computed from a truncated neighbourhood. An artefact along a seam that
is *visible* in a rendered view is recoverable — the user sees it. The same artefact absorbed into a
summary statistic is not.

Identifying the *kind* (1) matters because knowing output is approximate is insufficient when "sampled at
one point in sixty-four" and "computed without neighbours past the boundary" have different shapes: the
first is noise a user can reason about, the second is a localised error at a known place. [RFC-0003](../rfc/RFC-0003.md)
gives the taxonomy of reductions that produce each; this clause requires only that the kind be named,
so the obligation stands without it.

Propagation (2) prevents the disclosure being lost by composition: an exact aggregate over approximate
input is not an exact result.

(4) exists because (1) and (2) have an *operator* and a *pipeline* as their subjects, and neither covers the
third case: a pipeline of exact operators evaluated over less than the whole dataset. Without it,
[RFC-0003:C-RESOLUTION](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-resolution) 3 would oblige an evaluation to declare itself approximate "under (1)" while (1)
said nothing about evaluations — an obligation pointing at nothing. The three subjects are distinct and each
needs its own trigger.

### [RFC-0002:C-EXTENSION] Extension surface (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-extension"></a>

There is no plugin mechanism. An operator is written in-tree or by a consumer building against the published
crates, and everything else composes what already exists.

1. An operator MUST be implemented either in-tree or by a consumer depending on the published library crates
   and implementing their published interfaces.
   - A natively compiled library loaded at run time MUST NOT be admitted as an operator.
2. A pipeline MUST be expressible as the serialised document graph required by [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) 5.
   - A separate pipeline format MUST NOT be introduced alongside it.
3. An automation or scripting facility MUST NOT be able to introduce an operator.
   - It MAY compose registered operators and expressions (C-EXPRESSION), and nothing else.
4. Arbitrary user code MUST NOT be admitted as an operator.
   - Should a mechanism for it be introduced, that mechanism MUST supply the code's capabilities explicitly
     and MUST deny it ambient access, consistent with [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host).

#### Rationale

(1)'s prohibition on runtime-loaded native libraries is not a preference. Such a library has ambient
filesystem and network access, so it cannot satisfy [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host); it cannot exist on a target without
dynamic loading, so it breaks [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1; and a fault in it terminates the process holding
unsaved work. Why building against the crates is a real path rather than a consolation — and what the
rejected mechanisms were — is argued in the accompanying architecture decision.

(3) is the load-bearing restriction and the reason this clause is written before any automation facility
exists. A scripting layer that can introduce an operator is an escape hatch around every contract here, and
declining now is far easier than withdrawing later.

(4) is split so the presently-testable prohibition stands alone and the condition on any future mechanism
hangs beneath it. Only the prohibition is verifiable today; as one item, a compliance check could not tell
which half it was testing.

### [RFC-0002:C-EXPRESSION] Declarative expressions (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-expression"></a>

An attribute predicate is the most requested extension in any tool of this kind, and it is also the one form
of user-supplied logic that cannot break anything. That is not because it is checked; it is because the
contracts are unreachable from it.

1. An expression MUST be a pure function of a single point's attributes.
   - It MUST NOT perform input or output.
   - It MUST NOT retain state between evaluations.
   - It MUST NOT access any other point.
2. An expression MUST be evaluable vectorised over Arrow arrays.
   - It MUST NOT require per-point invocation of user-supplied code.
3. An operator parameterised by an expression MUST declare zero halo width and a single pass
   (C-EXEC 1).
4. Expression evaluation MUST be deterministic, so that a pipeline containing one still satisfies
   [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 2.

#### Rationale

(1)'s three sub-items are not a general purity requirement — each retires one specific obligation an
operator could otherwise violate silently, which is what makes an expression safe without any enforcement
machinery. Which obligations, and why that argument licences admitting expressions at all, is set out in the
accompanying architecture decision.

(2) is a scale requirement rather than a stylistic one. At billions of points, per-row invocation of an
interpreter is unusable, so an expression must compile to operations over whole arrays — which rules out
arbitrary control flow and user-defined calls, and so independently reinforces (1).

(3) follows from (1) rather than adding to it, and is stated so the planner can rely on it without inspecting
the expression.

### [RFC-0002:C-ORIGIN] Operator origin and verification (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-origin"></a>

Because a consumer may implement operators against the published interfaces, output may be produced by an
operator whose conformance nobody has checked. The contracts such an operator could break all fail silently,
so the fact must travel with the result.

1. Every registered operator MUST declare its origin, and whether its conformance has been verified in the
   sense defined by C-VERIFIED 1.
   - Verification status MUST NOT be asserted by the operator's own author.
2. A committed run MUST record the origin and verification status of every operator it evaluated, as part of
   the evaluation configuration [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 4 requires.
3. Output produced by an operator whose conformance is unverified MUST be surfaced to the user in the same
   manner as approximate output under C-APPROX 3.

#### Rationale

(1) depends on C-VERIFIED for its meaning rather than defining verification here, because
what must be verified is a property of the *operator contract* — halo sufficiency, memory ceiling, attribute
completeness, reduction determinism and its disclosure, approximation honesty — and those obligations live
in this RFC. A field
with no defined truth condition would not be testable, and defining it twice would let the definitions drift.

The nested prohibition exists because self-assertion would make the field decorative. An author confident
enough to publish an operator is confident enough to mark it verified, and the marker is only worth carrying
if it records independent confirmation.

(2) costs nothing: an evaluation configuration is already recorded for every committed run, so operator origin
is an addition to an existing record. It is what lets a forester defending a number say which operators
produced it and whether they were checked.

(3) is the substantive choice, and recording alone was the alternative. Recording alone means the user
discovers the provenance of a number after it is already in a report, with the decision already taken on it.
This is the same reasoning as C-APPROX 3 — a wrong number is indistinguishable from a right one,
so the signal has to arrive before the number is used. "Computed by an operator nobody verified" belongs in
the same category as "computed approximately".

### [RFC-0002:C-VERIFIED] What it means for an operator to be verified (Normative) <a id="rfc-0002c-verified"></a>

C-ORIGIN 1 requires an operator to declare whether its conformance has been verified, and a field with no
defined truth condition is not testable. What has to be checked is a property of the operator contract, so
the definition belongs here rather than with release policy.

1. An operator is **verified** when an assessor other than its author has confirmed each of:
   - that its declared halo width is sufficient for its neighbourhood definition (C-HALO 3);
   - that its peak memory conforms to its declared ceiling (C-MEMORY 1);
   - that its declared attribute set is complete (C-PROJECTION 3);
   - that any reduction it performs is independent of the degree of parallelism, the thread count and the
     partition size ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 8), that it reaches that property by the route
     [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 5 requires for its attribute rather than by whichever was convenient, and that
     it conforms to [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 7 in full where that route is associative accumulation;
   - that it does not rewrite attributes it passes through (C-MATERIALISATION 1);
   - that any summary it builds has an admissible declared size and is built where C-SUMMARY requires;
   - that it declares its output approximate where it diverges (C-APPROX 1).
2. An operator that has not been assessed against every item of (1) MUST be recorded as unverified.
   - Partial assessment MUST NOT be recorded as verification.

#### Rationale

The list is these seven and not a general appeal to quality because each is exactly one of the obligations an
operator can violate *silently* — an under-declared halo, an unbounded working set, an undeclared attribute
read, a reduction whose answer moves with the scheduler or whose accumulation quantum is unstated, an
attribute rewritten for no reason, an undisclosed approximation. Each fails without an error, which is why none can be left to whoever writes the next
operator to notice. Where an item has a mandated verification — C-HALO 4 and 6, C-MEMORY 5,
[RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 9, C-MATERIALISATION 4, C-MEMORY 5, C-SUMMARY 4, C-COMPOSITION 6 — what the assessor confirms
is that the verification was run and passed; where none exists, the assessor is the check.

The reduction item asks for the property *and* the route, which looks redundant and is not. There are two
ways to reach order independence, so an assessor checking only for fixed-order combination would reject a
conformant operator — but [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 5 is an obligation rather than a menu, so an assessor
checking only for the property would pass an operator that ordered-combines an attribute it was required to
accumulate associatively. Both errors are available and the item has to close both. Conformance to
[RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 7 is cited whole rather than by its declaration bullet because the half that matters
to a third party is the reporting, and citing only the declaration is how that half gets dropped.

The assessor-other-than-author requirement is what keeps the marker from being decorative. An author
confident enough to publish an operator is confident enough to self-certify, and the field is only worth
carrying if it records independent confirmation.

(2) closes the gap that would otherwise swallow (1): a partially assessed operator is indistinguishable from
a verified one unless partial assessment is explicitly not verification.
